chunks: Muhammad ibn Ali Majiluyah (may God be pleased with him) narrated to us, from his uncle Muhammad ibn Abi al-Qasim, from Ahmad ibn Abi Abdullah, from Ali ibn Muhammad, from Abu Ayyub al-Madani, from Suleiman ibn Ja'far al-Ja'fari, from al-Rida, from his forefathers, from Ali (peace be upon them) who said:
The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Learn three traits from the crow: its covering itself with dust, its early rising in search of sustenance, and its caution.'
ai.seo_question: What are the three traits of the crow that Muslims are encouraged to learn from according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In *Al-Khisal*, Shaykh al-Saduq records this hadith from Imam al-Rida (AS) to illustrate practical wisdom (*hikmah*) derived from nature, emphasizing that even animals possess virtues worthy of emulation. The three traits—modesty in privacy (*istitar*), early diligence in seeking sustenance (*bukhur*), and alertness to danger (*hazr*)—reflect key aspects of the Shia ethical ideal of balancing spiritual awareness with worldly prudence. This teaching underscores the Shia belief in the continuity of divine guidance through both revelation and the observant mind.

en.dr-ali-peiravi: 3-51 Muhammad ibn Ali Majiluyih - may God be pleased with him - narrated that his uncle Muhammad ibn Abil Qasim quoted on the authority of Ahmad ibn Aba Abdullah Al-Barqy, on the authority of Ali ibn Muhammad,on the authority of Abi Ayoob al-Madani, on the authority of Suleiman ibn Ja’far al-Ja’fari, on the authority of Al-Ridha (MGB), on the authority of his forefathers (MGB), on the authority of Ali (MGB) that God’s Prophet (MGB) said, “Learn three traits from the crow: having sex in private, going out after your daily bread early in the morning and being cautious.”
